entry.title: Grafana Loki: Log Aggregation That Indexes Labels, Not Lines

link.title: Grafana Loki: Log Aggregation That Indexes Labels, Not Lines

entry.content:
If you have ever trained a model overnight and woken up to a cryptic CUDA OOM at 3 a.m., you already know the real product of an ML system is not just the checkpoint — it is the log trail. Training jobs emit loss curves, data-loader warnings, NCCL timeout errors and GPU driver messages scattered across dozens of pods. Inference servers add request traces, latency warnings and quantization diagnostics on top. When something breaks, grep-ing SSH sessions across a dozen machines is not debugging, it is archaeology. Centralized log aggregation is the unglamorous infrastructure that turns that archaeology into a search box.

The catch is cost. Traditional log platforms build a full-text inverted index over every word you ship, which means storing roughly as much index as logs — often more. Grafana Loki takes the opposite road. Its README describes it in one line: “Loki: like Prometheus, but for logs.” Like Prometheus for metrics, Loki indexes only labels — the small key/value pairs such as job, app or pod that identify a stream — and stores the log lines themselves compressed and unindexed. Searching inside lines happens at query time, by scanning. That trade makes the write path fast, the storage bill small, and the operational burden light, at the price of slower full-text scans. Queries reuse the exact label vocabulary you already use for metrics, and if you run Grafana you can flip between metrics and logs without changing mental models.

This post is a source tour of the Loki repository (branch main, module github.com/grafana/loki/v3), focused on the Go code that makes that idea real: the distributor that receives your logs, the ingester that buffers and flushes them, the LogQL engine that answers queries, and the storage layer that indexes labels and nothing else. I mapped both the write path and the read path into two diagrams; every symbol cited below was located in the actual source at a verified line number.

Overview: one binary, four roles. The module manager wires the push handler, ingester, querier, LogQL engine and ruler over a shared TSDB index and object storage.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L138 — the cmd/loki binary parses its config wrapper and calls loki.New, then t.Run at L149 starts every service for the selected -target.
  • Loki struct, L446 — the root datastructure holding the server, ring, overrides and every component; setupModuleManager at L798 builds the dependency graph between modules.
  • initDistributor, L341 — wires the push HTTP handler at L393 and routes POST /loki/api/v1/push at L403.
  • Distributor.Push, L508 — the write entry point: validates each stream, shards streams by label hash and replicates them to ingesters over gRPC.
  • instance.Push, L231 — the per-tenant ingester instance appends entries into compressed in-memory chunks and logs a record to the WAL at L265.
  • query.Exec, L273 — the LogQL engine executes instant and range queries, deferring to an evaluator built by NewDefaultEvaluator at L310.
  • SelectLogs, L217 — the querier merges still-buffered logs from ingesters with long-term store reads; SelectSamples at L290 serves the metric side of LogQL.
  • NewStore, L132 — the LokiStore (type at L99) fans each query out over schema periods, using a per-period index and chunk client.

Detail view: from HTTP push and the distributor's validation flow, through ingester streams, chunk cuts and the WAL, into the LogQL engine, querier fan-out, TSDB index and object storage.

From Install to Your First Model

Loki ships as a single Go binary with no external dependencies, which is exactly what you want when the machines you care about are GPU nodes that should not be running a zookeeper of their own. The README’s build-from-source path is three commands: clone the repository, build with go build ./cmd/loki, and run ./loki -config.file=./cmd/loki/loki-local-config.yaml (both commands are shown verbatim in the repository README, lines 108-111). The checked-in local config listens on http_listen_port: 3100 (line 4 of cmd/loki/loki-local-config.yaml), which is the one port you need to remember; gRPC sits next to it on 9096.

Readiness is a plain HTTP check: the root Loki struct registers a GET /ready handler at loki.go L638 that flips to 200 once all modules report healthy. In a Kubernetes launcher this is your startup probe. Getting logs in is a single HTTP call — the push route is the constant PathLokiPush = "/loki/api/v1/push" defined at api_paths.go L34 — and the same endpoint accepts OpenTelemetry payloads through a dedicated OTLP handler at http.go L36, so an OpenTelemetry Collector sidecar can forward trace-adjacent log records without any Loki-specific agent. The repository README also documents LogCLI, a small command-line client for running queries like a stream selector against your instance.

Your first query is then a label selector. In LogQL, curly braces pick streams the way they do in PromQL: something like a selector on job or pod returns every line of those streams in the time range, and you can layer filters and metric expressions on top — wrap the selector in rate(...) or count matches per minute — without ever leaving the same query language your dashboards use. For a training fleet this pays off immediately: one query template per job name surfaces driver errors from every node, and the same labels that showed you GPU utilization in Prometheus now show you the logs around each spike.

Inside the Write Path: Distributor to Ingester

A push request lands at the distributor, and the first thing that happens is not storage — it is judgment. Distributor.Push at L508 resolves the tenant from the context and hands the request to pushWithResolver at L520, which walks every stream, enforces per-tenant limits such as ingestion rate and label length, optionally shards streams that exceed their rate budget, and computes each stream’s hash key from its labels. The hash is what the consistent ring uses to pick which ingester replicas own the stream. Rejected streams never leave the distributor, and the response reports what was dropped.

The receiving ingester is deliberately simple: Ingester.Push at ingester.go L1018 checks whether the WAL disk is throttled, then dispatches to a per-tenant instance. Inside the instance at instance.go L231, streams are looked up or created — createStream at L283 parses the label set and applies stream-count limits — and entries are appended by stream.Push at stream.go L168. Lines accumulate in a compressed in-memory chunk; when the chunk fills, cutChunk at L492 seals it for the flusher. Before any of that is acked, the instance writes a record to the WAL (wal.Log call at instance.go L265), so a crash between memory and object storage costs you nothing. The WAL interface itself lives at wal.go L63.

Two design choices matter here. First, chunks are grouped by label set: all lines with identical labels share a stream, which is why high-cardinality labels blow up both memory and index — a theme the limits section returns to. Second, the write path is O(labels), not O(lines): line text is only compressed, never parsed for indexing, so the cost per gigabyte stays flat no matter how chatty your training logs are.

Inside the Read Path: LogQL Down to Chunks

Queries enter through the same module wiring but take the opposite route. The querier module (initQuerier at modules.go L520) builds a query API at L642 and instantiates the LogQL engine via logql.NewEngine at L2298. The engine type at engine.go L208 parses your query into an AST (ParseExpr at syntax/parser.go L62), then query.Exec at L273 instruments the run and delegates to the evaluator, which pulls data through the Querier interface.

The SingleTenantQuerier (type at querier.go L165) is the fan-out point, and its constructor signature at L186 is a quiet announcement of the storage transition: it takes both a classic chunk store and a new data-object store. For log queries, SelectLogs at L217 merges two sources — the IngesterQuerier (type at ingester_querier.go L50), which asks live ingesters for unflushed streams, and the long-term store. Metric queries call SelectSamples at L290 with the same dual sources. The merge means Loki answers over the last few minutes and the last few months with one query and no special-casing in your dashboard.

Storage: Index the Labels, Compress the Lines

The store is where the “index only labels” promise is kept. LokiStore at store.go L99 is schema-aware: Loki’s config lets different time periods use different index and chunk backends, and NewStore at L132 assembles a client per period. SelectLogs at L531 walks the period configs that overlap the query range, and each one consults the index — the TSDB single-store index whose builder lives under pkg/storage/stores/shipper/indexshipper/tsdb/builder.go — to turn label matchers into a list of chunk references. Only then are the referenced objects fetched, through the chunk client built by NewChunkClient at factory.go L354 on top of the object client from NewObjectClient at L415 (S3, GCS, Azure, or plain filesystem — a MinIO bucket works fine for a homelab). The index is small because it maps labels and stream time ranges, not words; the chunks are big but cheap because they are just compressed bytes.

The tree also shows where the project is heading. A columnar object format lives at pkg/dataobj/dataobj.go (the Object type at L89), with builder, compaction and metastore modules registered in the module table — a storage engine that keeps data in open columnar objects instead of the classic chunk-plus-index split. Bloom filters for line-level pruning ship under pkg/storage/bloom/v1 with a dedicated shipper. The ruler — built by NewRuler at ruler.go L14 and wired at modules.go L1458 — reuses the exact same LogQL engine (see createRulerQueryEngine touching the engine at L1548), so the query you debug interactively is the query your alert evaluates on a schedule.

Honest Limits

Loki’s economy has a price, and it is worth naming before you commit a fleet to it. Label-only indexing means anything inside the line is found by scanning: a query that filters on a rare string across a week of logs will touch far more data than the same search in ClickHouse, which indexes aggressively and answers ad-hoc full-text in milliseconds — but pays for that with a heavier cluster and a real database to operate. If your workflow is “grep anything, anytime, forever,” Loki will feel slow at large ranges. If it is “show me logs for this pod around the CPU spike,” it feels instant.

The second limit is cardinality, self-inflicted by design. Every unique label combination is a stream with its own index entries and its own in-memory buffer, so slapping a UUID or a request ID into labels multiplies streams until the ingester rejects writes. The rule of thumb the project repeats: keep identifiers in the log line, keep stable attributes in labels. Third, WAL-replay restarts are real: an ingester that crashes replays its WAL before serving, and while replication covers you, a monolithic single-binary deployment trades that safety for simplicity. Fourth, the repository is in visible motion — the distributor/ingester/querier packages have just moved out of pkg/loki to the repository root (pkg/distributor, pkg/ingester, pkg/querier), and the data-object storage engine is under active construction, so file paths in this tour will drift with the tree. None of that changes the core bet: for ML teams that already run Prometheus and Grafana, Loki turns the log trail of a failed training run into a label query — and keeps the storage bill small enough that you can afford to keep every epoch’s logs.

entry.title: Inside Memcached: The C Event Machine That Still Wins the Latency Game

link.title: Inside Memcached: The C Event Machine That Still Wins the Latency Game

entry.content:
If you build anything around models, you spend your life answering the same question over and over: the same prompt prefix, the same tokenizer call, the same feature vector, the same session lookup. Doing that work twice is pure waste, and at inference scale waste is measured in GPUs. That is why the humble in-memory cache is quietly one of the most load-bearing components of modern ML infrastructure: an embedding cache turns repeated encoding requests into sub-millisecond hash lookups, a tokenization cache keeps your preprocessor from re-splitting the same corpus a thousand times, and a session store keeps state off stateless inference servers. Before Redis, before Valkey, there was Memcached — and its C source is still one of the best teaching artifacts in open source.

Memcached describes itself as a “high performance multithreaded event-based key/value cache store intended to be used in a distributed system”, and the entire project fits in a handful of C files at the root of the repository. There is no scripting engine in the core, no persistence by default, no clusters-from-the-box. The philosophy is radical simplicity: hash a key, find an item, hand it back, and evict old data when memory runs out. Everything else — consistency, partitioning, serialization — is deliberately left to the client. That refusal to grow is exactly why it remains a default choice for LRU-style caching fleets two decades in.

This post walks the actual source tree on master with two generated architecture diagrams: an overview of the request flow, and a deeper map covering the protocols, memory management, flash offload, LRU crawler and the newer proxy layer. Every symbol below is linked to its real line on GitHub, so you can read along in the code as we go.

The overview: a client connection is accepted, handed to a worker thread, parsed by the text or meta protocol layer, and answered from the slab-allocated hash table — with a flash fallback for oversized items.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L4714 parses flags like -p, -m and -t, initializes the slab allocator and threads, then settles into the libevent loop that never returns.
  • conn_new, L610 wraps each accepted socket in a conn struct and attaches it to an event base; this is also where proxy-mode connections get their own read handler installed.
  • drive_machine, L2965 is the beating heart: a while (!stop) loop that walks a connection through listening, waiting, reading, parsing and writing states.
  • dispatch_conn_new, L772 spreads new connections across worker threads via their notify pipes, so no single thread owns the listening socket queue.
  • process_command_ascii, L1529 is the dispatcher for both the classic text protocol and the modern meta commands (mg, ms, md, ma, me).
  • do_item_alloc, L249 carves a new item out of the slab allocator sized to the key-plus-value, while do_slabs_alloc, L411 hands out the actual chunk.
  • assoc_find, L70 walks the chained hash bucket for the key — the single most executed data structure operation in the daemon.

The detail map: protocols and parsers on one side, slab and LRU machinery in the middle, and the extstore flash path, LRU crawler and Lua proxy at the edges.

The Event Loop Is a State Machine

Most servers you read will have a handler-per-request structure. Memcached does something older and, in my opinion, more elegant: every connection is a tiny state machine, and drive_machine, L2965 is the single function that advances all of them. The switch (c->state) covers conn_listening (accept with accept4), conn_waiting, conn_read (via try_read_network, L2431), conn_parse_cmd, conn_nread (copying the value bytes into the item with complete_nread, L1422), conn_mwrite and conn_closing.

Two details in that loop reward attention. First, conn_new_cmd decrements a per-event request budget (nreqs, seeded from settings.reqs_per_event) so a single chatty connection cannot starve the rest of the worker — the loop yields and lets libevent re-arm instead. Second, the same state machine drives listener sockets and client sockets alike; a listening conn simply sits in conn_listening and accepts, then dispatch_conn_new ships the client fd to a worker. The threading model is one lock-free event loop per worker thread, each owning a slice of connections, with a short mutexed section whenever the shared hash table is touched. It is the original “threads plus epoll” recipe, and reading it makes most modern async frameworks look overdressed.

One Daemon, Three Dialects

The protocol surface is where the code has grown the most, and the dispatcher process_command_ascii, L1529 shows all of it in one switch. Parsing itself was recently unified in process_request, L163, a shared tokenizer that extracts the key, flags, TTL and value length for both classic and meta commands.

The classic text protocol is still what most people learn first: get, set, gets route through process_get_command, L429 and process_update_command, L764, the latter calling into the shared process_update_cmd_start in the parser which allocates the item before the value bytes are read. The meta protocol (mg, ms, md, ma, me, mn) is the modern surface — compact, flag-driven, and finally able to express things like “return TTL with the value” or “vivify the key if missing” without new verbs. The mg path in process_mget_cmd, L984 is worth reading in full: flag letters (v, f, t, c, k, N, J) each map to behavior, including on-the-fly item creation for the vivify case.

The binary protocol lives in proto_bin.c, where try_read_command_binary, L49 validates the fixed 24-byte header and dispatch_bin_command, L897 switches over opcodes, including the SASL authentication commands. And since this is a cache used in front of fleets, there is a fourth dialect that is not even a client dialect: when the server is built with --enable-proxy (documented in the README), proxy-mode connections get try_read_command_proxy, L605 installed as their read handler, and requests flow into the Lua-based router instead of the local hash table.

Slabs, LRU and the Hash Table

Memory management is the part of Memcached that has barely changed since the beginning, because it is hard to beat. The allocator slabs.c pre-sorts memory into slab classes, each holding pages carved into fixed-size chunks; the growth factor and minimum chunk size are the -f and -n flags you see in usage, L4008. When a value needs storing, do_item_alloc, L249 asks do_slabs_alloc, L411 for a chunk from the right class, and when items die, do_slabs_free, L501 returns the chunk to its freelist. No coalescing, no compaction — fragmentation is contained by design because chunks within a class are uniform.

On top of the allocator sits a classic pair: a chained hash table and per-LRU-class eviction. The hash function is pluggable at startup via hash_init, L15 — jenkins, murmur3 or the modern xxh3 default — and inserts go through assoc_insert, L153 while lookups walk buckets in assoc_find, L70. The item itself is linked into an LRU by do_item_link, L485, and when memory is tight or items expire, lru_pull_tail, L1072 sweeps the tail of a given LRU: evicting, unlinking through assoc_delete, L172, and recycling the chunk. Refcounts, not locks, keep an item alive while a reader finishes with it — a pattern worth stealing for your own code.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s build instructions are refreshingly short, and they still work. For a from-source build you need autotools and libevent (on Debian: sudo apt-get install autotools-dev automake libevent-dev), then:

cd memcached
./autogen.sh
./configure
make
make test

The binary lands in the same folder. Start it with a memory cap and a thread count tuned to your box — -m sets item memory in megabytes, -t the worker threads, -p the TCP port (defaults to 11211), all documented in the usage text:

./memcached -m 2048 -t 4 -p 11211 -u nobody

Then the README’s own smoke test: telnet 127.0.0.1 11211 and type stats. Because the text protocol is exactly that — text — your first cache round-trip needs nothing more than a shell. Once connected, set greeting 0 0 5 followed by hello stores a value, and get greeting brings it back; you can see every one of these verbs handled in proto_text.c. From Python, a two-line client (telnetlib for a demo, or pymemcache in production) is enough to front your tokenizer or embedding service with a shared fleet: point several app servers at one host string, and keys collide into a single namespace. For the AI workloads above the sweet spot is exactly what the code shows: hot, small, immutable values with a TTL. If you need persistence, streams or rich data types, that is a different tool — see the tour of Redis or its libre fork Valkey — and if you are wiring the cache into request handlers, the FastAPI source tour shows the app side of that integration.

Flash, Crawler, Proxy: The Modern Edges

Three newer subsystems extend the classic core without contaminating it. The first is extstore, enabled with --enable-extstore and isolated in extstore.c: a background writer thread in storage_write, L499 pulls cold items off the COLD_LRU tail, allocates a tiny header item to stay in RAM, and streams the body to flash pages through extstore_write, L652. A read of such an item goes through storage_get_item, L252, which submits an async I/O back into the event loop — RAM prices be damned, this is how you keep a 100 GB embedding cache without 100 GB of DRAM.

The second is the LRU crawler in crawler.c: instead of letting expiration happen lazily on access, lru_crawler metadump or lru_crawler crawl all (parsed by process_lru_crawler_command, L1287 and started in lru_crawler_crawl, L933) walks LRU tails in the background, expiring dead items and even streaming key metadata for debugging.

The third is the proxy layer under proto_proxy.c and its siblings: once enabled, proxy_process_command, L966 builds a request object and runs it through proxy_run_rcontext, L818, a Lua execution context where you write routing functions — pool selection, key prefixing, retries, shadow reads. It turns a fleet of memcached boxes into one logical cache with client-side unawareness, which for large embedding stores is the difference between one hot node and a ring.

Honest Limits

Memcached is honest about what it is not, and so should you be. There is no persistence and no replication: restart the daemon and the cache is empty by definition, which is why warm-up scripts and request coalescing on your app tier matter. There is no server-side cluster coordination — partitioning is done by client hashing, so resizing a fleet historically caused cache misses until consistent hashing (or the proxy with its jump/ring hash modules) entered the picture. Values must fit a slab class; very large blobs waste memory unless extstore is enabled, and the classic 1 MB default value cap still shapes how people model data. Expiration is per-item with a TTL, but there are no key tags or group invalidation in the core, so cache invalidation for a corpus refresh means application-level namespacing. And while the meta protocol is a genuine improvement, huge parts of the internet’s tooling still speak the old text protocol, so you will meet both — usually in the same codebase. Use it for what it is — the fastest boring layer between your model and a recompute — and let the diagram above be your map the next time stats output looks like a wall of numbers.

entry.title: NATS: The Featherweight Messaging Backbone for Distributed AI

link.title: NATS: The Featherweight Messaging Backbone for Distributed AI

entry.content:
Every serious AI system turns into a fan-out problem embarrassingly fast. One “answer the user” request becomes a burst of calls to an embedding service, a retriever, a reranker, and a model provider; a training run becomes millions of checkpoint, metric, and gradient events; an agent becomes a swarm of workers that need to talk to each other more than they talk to you. Wiring all of that with direct HTTP calls produces a hairball of retries, timeouts, and service discovery. What you actually want is a small, fast post office in the middle: services publish events on subjects, other services subscribe, and nobody keeps a phone book of everyone else’s addresses. That is the niche NATS owns, and unlike heavyweight log brokers such as Kafka, it does so with a single Go binary that will happily run on a Raspberry Pi at the edge of your cluster.

NATS is a CNCF project with a simple pitch: a “simple, secure and performant communications system for digital systems, services and devices,” backed by over 40 client language implementations. The core protocol is text-based and at-most-once — blazing fast fire-and-forget pub/sub with request-reply semantics. On top of that sits JetStream, the built-in persistence layer that turns the same server into a durable, replayable stream store with exactly-once-ish consumer semantics, which makes it a lighter alternative to a dedicated log broker when your durability needs are modest. Security, JWT-based accounts, clustering, gateways, and leaf nodes are all part of the same server, not sidecar plugins.

In this post we read the actual Go source of nats-io/nats-server on the main branch (currently pre-release 2.16.0-dev) and follow a message from a TCP socket to a subscriber — and then to disk, to other servers in a cluster, and to edge nodes. Both diagrams below were generated directly from the repository, so every node links to the real file on GitHub.

NATS at a glance: connections on the left, the subject-trie routing core in the middle, JetStream persistence below, and cluster/edge propagation plus HTTP monitoring on the right.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Server.Start, L2294 — the bootstrap function: it opens the client listener, monitoring server, route accept loop, gateways, leaf node listeners, and JetStream, each in its own goroutine.
  • readLoop, L1503 — one goroutine per connection drains the socket into the parser; the same client struct serves plain clients, routes, gateways, and leaf nodes, differentiated by a kind field.
  • parse, L137 — a hand-rolled state machine that turns raw bytes into OP_CONNECT, OP_PUB, OP_SUB, OP_PING operations without allocating per protocol token.
  • processPub, L3016 — the publish path: validate subject and payload, then hand the message to the fan-out machinery; its sibling processSub, L3121 registers subscriptions.
  • Sublist.Match, L555 — resolution of a subject like orders.*.created against a token trie, with a cache for hot subjects; Insert at L375 maintains the tree.
  • EnableJetStream, L207 — wires the storage directory, system accounts, and encryption keys; once enabled, $JS.API requests are served by apiDispatch, L951.
  • processJetStreamMsg, L6486 — the stream engine’s ingest: de-duplication, retention limits, and a hand-off to the storage backend, where StoreMsg, L5579 appends into on-disk message blocks.
  • connectToRoute, L2933 — how servers find each other: solicited and gossip-discovered routes exchange INFO and sync subscription interest so a publish on one node reaches subscribers everywhere.
  • HandleRoot, L1523 — the monitoring port’s index page, linking the JSON endpoints (/varz, /connz, /jsz, and friends) that operators scrape.

The detailed map: config and lifecycle, the per-connection read loop, interest and auth, the JetStream stack with its storage backends and Raft replication, clustering and edge topology, and the monitoring surface.

From Install to Your First Pub/Sub

NATS is a textbook Go module — the repository root declares module github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2 in go.mod, L1 with a package main entry point at main.go, L14, so the standard go install github.com/nats-io/nats-server/v2@latest drops a single nats-server binary onto your path. Prebuilt binaries and Docker images are also published per release; the README itself is notably spare and points you to the official docs at docs.nats.io rather than embedding a quick start. Run the binary with no arguments and it listens for client connections on port 4222 — that default lives in code as DEFAULT_PORT, L78 and surfaces again in the CLI help, where usageStr, L27 documents -p, --port for clients and -m, --http_port for monitoring.

Because the protocol is plain text over TCP, you do not even need a client library to prove it works. telnet localhost 4222 greets you with an INFO line; send:

CONNECT {"verbose":false}
SUB inference.done 1

then from a second terminal:

PUB inference.done 11
hello world

and the first terminal prints MSG inference.done 1 11 followed by the payload. Those are not toy approximations — the exact OP_PUB, OP_SUB, and OP_MSG states of this protocol are enumerated in the parser starting at L75. For real applications, install the nats CLI and any of the 40+ client libraries, and the same subjects work unchanged. When you want durability, add a config file with jetstream: enabled and store_dir, pass it with -c, and Options.ProcessConfigFile, L1084 will validate everything before startup — changes to many settings can even be applied live through Server.Reload, L1438 without dropping connections.

The Read Loop: How a PUB Becomes a Fan-out

The elegance of the NATS server is that the hot path is almost embarrassingly direct. A connection’s readLoop, L1503 reads from the socket in growing buffers and feeds parse, L137, which keeps a per-client parse state and calls back into the client methods as operations complete. A CONNECT triggers processConnect, L2346, which authenticates the connection through checkAuthentication, L415 — supporting tokens, username/password, NKeys, and JWT-decoded accounts — and binds the client to its Account struct, L51.

Here is the trick that keeps routing fast: there is no global subscription table. Every account owns its own Sublist trie (the sl field at L70), so subject lookups stay cache-friendly and tenants cannot bloat each other’s match times. On publish, processPub, L3016 resolves the subject locally and processMsgResults, L5368 walks the matched subscription set, and for each target deliverMsg, L3854 appends the message to the subscriber’s outbound queue. Slow consumers are handled by capping those queues and, when a client falls too far behind, marking it a “slow consumer” rather than stalling the publisher — a deliberate choice that keeps the fast path lock-light and non-blocking.

JetStream: Streams, Consumers, and the File Store

Flipping on JetStream changes the story from “deliver and forget” to “store, replicate, and replay.” Streams are created over the same pub/sub fabric: a client publishes to $JS.API.STREAM.CREATE..., apiDispatch, L951 matches the request to a handler, and the stream registers an internal subscription so that ordinary publishes on its bound subjects land in processJetStreamMsg, L6486. There the engine applies de-duplication windows, per-stream limits (messages, bytes, age), and retention policy before calling into storage.

Storage behind JetStream is pluggable through the StreamStore interface, L95, with two in-tree implementations: memory (memStore.StoreMsg, L407) for ephemeral streams and the file store (StoreMsg, L5579) for durable ones. The file store is the crown jewel of this codebase — roughly fifteen thousand lines managing append-only message blocks with CRCs, optional at-rest encryption, async flush, and on-restart recovery, which is why a stream survives a crash or a rolling upgrade. Consumers read from that state: consumer.deliverMsg, L5895 sequences messages out to pull or push subscribers and tracks acknowledgements, so replaying from an arbitrary sequence is just re-walking the store. If you have followed our write-ups on log-structured systems like Loki, the shape will feel familiar — append-optimized blocks, coarse indexes, cheap sequential reads.

Clustering, Gateways, and Leaf Nodes

Single-server NATS is already useful, but the topology features are what make it fit AI deployments that sprawl across datacenters. Within a cluster, servers connect to each other as routes: startRouteAcceptLoop, L2738 accepts inbound route connections and addRoute, L2145 registers them. Discovery can be configured or gossip-style — servers announce themselves via processImplicitRoute, L1056 and relay new peer info with forwardNewRouteInfoToKnownServers, L1152, so you seed each node with a couple of addresses and the mesh self-assembles. Subscription interest propagates along routes so publishes traverse only links that actually lead to subscribers.

For JetStream itself, clustering means consensus: enabling it via enableJetStreamClustering, L1297 puts stream and consumer assignments under a Raft meta group, where Propose, L1048 replicates entries and elections pick the leader that owns each stream. Above clusters sit gateways — startGatewayAcceptLoop, L491 links independent clusters with interest-propagated messaging, useful for region-to-region fan-out. And below sit leaf nodes: startLeafNodeAcceptLoop, L1088 accepts edge servers, while a remote leaf dials home through connectToRemoteLeafNodeAsynchronously, L786. A leaf node keeps working when disconnected — your edge inference box keeps serving local subjects — and rejoins the hub later, which is exactly the model you want for a fleet of GPU nodes behind flaky links, à la Ray workers.

Monitoring the Server

Start the server with -m 8222 (the flag documented in main.go, L35) and you get an HTTP monitoring endpoint whose index is rendered by HandleRoot, L1523 — a deliberately plain HTML page listing the JSON endpoints. Varz, L1635 reports configuration and runtime stats, Connz, L205 lists live connections with their subscriptions and pending bytes, and Jsz, L3294 summarizes JetStream streams, consumers, and store usage. There is no built-in dashboard; the design assumption is that Prometheus scrapes these endpoints and Grafana draws the graphs — the same observability stack we described for OpenTelemetry-style setups. Beyond polling, the server emits system advisories on $SYS subjects via sendInternalMsg, L763, so connect events, account stats, and JetStream warnings can simply be subscribed to by an ops tool.

Honest Limits

NATS trades generality for focus, and it is worth being explicit about the edges. Core NATS is at-most-once: if a subscriber is slow or disconnected, it misses messages, period — JetStream is mandatory for anything you cannot afford to lose, and running it means managing store directories, block files, and cluster quorums. The README is famously minimal: no quick start, no benchmarks, no tuning guide — the real documentation lives on docs.nats.io. The monitoring story is JSON endpoints plus whatever dashboards you build yourself; do not expect a turnkey UI. JetStream’s Raft clustering adds operational surface — meta-group elections, peer cleanup, snapshot management — that a two-node setup will not teach you, so plan for at least three servers. And the subject-trie model rewards careful naming: wildcard-heavy subjects with low locality can pressure the match cache, so schema discipline matters more than it looks. Finally, production still wants TLS, JWT account boundaries, and resource limits configured thoughtfully — the code paths exist (checkAuthentication, L415 among them) but none are sensible defaults you can ignore.

None of that diminishes the core appeal: a ~15 MB Go binary that turns any VM, container, or Raspberry Pi into a messaging fabric with optional durability, honest clustering, and a protocol you can debug over telnet. For AI workloads built around fan-out inference, agent coordination, and event-driven data collection, NATS is often the smallest component that quietly carries the most traffic — and now you have the map of how it does it.

entry.title: Inside the OpenTelemetry Collector: The Go Engine That Routes Every Trace, Metric and Log

link.title: Inside the OpenTelemetry Collector: The Go Engine That Routes Every Trace, Metric and Log

entry.content:
Modern AI systems are telemetry furnaces. An LLM gateway emits metrics that classic web apps never had: tokens per second, time-to-first-token, queue depth per model replica, cache hit ratios on a prompt store. Every step of an agent — tool call, retrieval hit, retry — wants to be a span. GPU hosts want to report utilization, thermal events and batch occupancy as metrics, and the debugging session that starts with a hallucination usually ends with you reading traces at three in the morning. The hard part is not generating these signals; your frameworks already do. The hard part is moving them: different shapes, different backends, batching under bursty load, retries, tail sampling, redaction of prompts that may contain user data. That plumbing problem is exactly what the OpenTelemetry Collector was built to solve. Its README describes it plainly: a vendor-agnostic implementation of how to receive, process and export telemetry data — one binary that stands between your AI services and every backend you use, from Jaeger to Kafka to a managed vendor.

There are two repositories people conflate. open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector — the subject of this post — is the engine: the component interfaces, the OTLP-native data model, the config system, the service runtime that turns YAML into a directed graph of running components, and the otelcol binary itself. The sibling opentelemetry-collector-contrib repository is the long tail: hundreds of receivers, processors, exporters and connectors, from PostgreSQL scrapers to Kafka brokers. If you have ever added a component to a config file and wondered what actually happens next, the machinery lives in the core repo — and that is the machinery we are going to read, file by file, with line anchors into the main branch.

We will do it in two passes. The overview diagram below follows a signal from the command line to the exporter. The detail diagram then opens every stage up: the collector lifecycle, config resolution, the service graph internals, and the three pdata signal containers. Every symbol mentioned in the text links to the real source, verified in the repo as of today.

Figure 1 — The 10,000-meter view: the otelcol binary builds a Collector, which resolves configuration and hands component factories to the Service, which assembles a directed acyclic graph of receivers, processors and exporters that exchange pdata signals.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • NewCommand, L25 — the cobra root command is the binary’s front door; its RunE constructs a Collector and calls Run.
  • Collector struct, L100 — the process owner: settings, config provider, the Service, state and shutdown channels.
  • ConfigProvider.Get, L55 — serves the configuration on demand and on change.
  • Resolver.Resolve, L164 — fetches each config URI through a provider, merges the maps and expands references.
  • service.New, L108 — builds internal telemetry, extensions and the component graph.
  • graph.Build, L78 — turns the service config into a DAG of component instances.
  • receiverNode, L26 — one graph node per receiver instance, wired to the next consumers.
  • Traces, L21 — the pdata container every component actually passes around.

Figure 2 — The full plumbing: CLI and lifecycle, the confmap resolution stack, the service runtime, the data flow graph with its virtual nodes, and the pdata signal containers that carry your LLM metrics, agent spans and logs.

A Vendor-Agnostic Router, in One Binary

Everything starts in otelcol/. NewCommand, L25 assembles a cobra command whose RunE constructs NewCollector, L129 and then blocks in Collector.Run, L414. Command-line surface is deliberately tiny: flags.go registers the config flag, L15 — repeatable, one location per entry — plus a --set override flag at L39. Two diagnostic subcommands round it out: otelcol components (newComponentsCommand, L45) prints every factory baked into the binary from the Factories, L21 struct, and a validate subcommand (L13) checks a config without running it.

The Collector struct, L100 walks through four states, StateStarting through StateClosed (L30), and its Run method is just a startup call followed by a select loop: it waits on the config watcher (L464), on asynchronous component errors, on SIGHUP/SIGINT/SIGTERM, and on the channel closed by Collector.Shutdown, L166. Config change or reload signal triggers reloadConfiguration, L289, which tears down the retiring Service and builds a new one — with a partial-reload fast path (UpdateReceivers, L273) that restarts only the receivers that actually changed and leaves the rest of the graph untouched. For a long-running AI gateway this means you can tune processors without dropping in-flight signals.

The Config Layer: From a URI to a Struct

The Collector never reads files itself. ConfigProvider, L23 wraps a confmap.Resolver and exposes Get/Watch/Shutdown. Inside the resolver, Resolve, L164 retrieves each configured location through a pluggable Provider interface, L54, merges the resulting maps in order, runs converters, and expands references like ${env:OTEL_KEY}. The scheme dispatch is the elegant part: a file provider whose scheme is literally “file”, L18, an env provider, L21, plus http/https and yaml providers out of the box. Watching is symmetric: Resolver.Watch, L258 returns a channel that fires when any watched location changes.

The resolved map is unmarshalled into otelcol.Config, L22 — top-level maps for receivers, exporters, processors, connectors and extensions, plus the service section — and validated by Config.Validate, L49: an empty file is an error, at least one receiver and one exporter must be configured, and every component referenced by the service section must exist. Fail here and the process exits before any component is built.

The Service Graph: A DAG, Not a Chain

This is the part most people get wrong about the Collector. It is not a linear chain; it is a directed acyclic graph, assembled at runtime by the service/internal/graph package. service.New, L108 first creates the internal telemetry (resource, logger, meter and tracer providers), then calls initGraph, L340, which feeds builders and the configured signal flows into graph.Build, L78.

Build runs three phases. createNodes, L101 adds one node per component instance — receivers and exporters are deduplicated across flows of the same signal, processors are unique per flow, and connectors (connectorNode, L31) are type-checked so an exporter on one signal always pairs with a receiver on another. createEdges, L268 then wires each flow: receivers emit into a virtual capabilitiesNode, L20 that aggregates whether the flow mutates data, the processors are chained in config order, and a fanOutNode, L15 sits before the exporters so one signal can fan out to many backends. Finally buildComponents, L297 topologically sorts the graph (topo.Sort, L298) and instantiates real components in reverse order, handing each one its nextConsumers, L378 — this is the moment a receiver receives the consumer it will push spans into.

Startup respects the DAG: StartAll, L406 starts downstream components first so every consumer is ready before its producer (Service.Start, L232 starts extensions, then the graph, then logs the famous “Everything is ready” line), and ShutdownAll, L467 stops in the opposite order so components drain cleanly. The Host, L31 ties it together as the component.Host implementation, answering factory lookups (GetFactory, L48), status reporting and zPages.

From Install to Your First Model

From install to first flowing signal takes about five minutes, and it doubles as a working mental model of the whole machine — your first model of how telemetry moves.

  1. Download a distro binary. The README links the releases page, where the project publishes signed artifacts (cosign verification is documented in the README). Container images otel/opentelemetry-collector are published under the same release process.
  2. Write a minimal config. One OTLP receiver (gRPC on 4317, HTTP on 4318) and the debug exporter are the classic starting pair:
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
exporters:
  debug:
    verbosity: detailed
service:
  telemetry:
    logs:
      level: info
  # under the service section you also declare your signal flows:
  # for each of traces, metrics and logs, list which receivers feed
  # which exporters, with optional processors between them.
  # The getting-started guide shows the exact stanza.
  1. Run it: otelcol --config=config.yaml. The config flag is the one requirement — command.go rejects a start without it, L61. For the precise service stanza, the official getting-started guide (linked from the README) walks through the exact flow declaration.
  2. Push one signal through. Any OTLP client will do — curl a JSON span to port 4318, or point a Python opentelemetry-sdk tracer at it. The debug exporter prints the pdata you just created, and you can literally watch your span travel receiver → capabilities node → fan-out → exporter, exactly as the diagram promised.

For an AI stack this scales up naturally: point your LLM gateway’s OTLP endpoint at the Collector, add a batch processor to absorb traffic spikes, and export metrics to Prometheus, traces to Jaeger, or mirror raw signals onto Kafka when a downstream consumer wants its own replay. Same binary, same graph, one config file.

pdata: Where Every Signal Lives

Every component in that graph speaks one in-memory language: pdata. The package doc says it directly — pdata defines the data model for all supported signals, L6. It is a hand-written Go mirror of the OTLP protobufs: Traces, L21 is a wrapper around resource-span slices (ResourceSpans, L49), Logs, L21 and Metrics, L21 follow the same resource → scope → record layering, and pcommon.Map, L18 with Range, L242 is the attribute bag they all share, alongside a fixed-size TraceID, L15. At the wire edge, ExportRequest, L17 wraps a Traces value for gRPC/HTTP transport without re-copying the data.

Why does a dedicated model matter? Because signals cross many component boundaries on their way through the graph, and re-serializing at each hop would be ruinous. pdata lets a receiver hand a mutable structure to a processor and on to an exporter with zero copies of the payload between them — but mutability is tracked: the capabilities node computes whether anything downstream mutates data, and the receiver side clones defensively when it does. When you build AI-specific processors (prompt redaction, token-cost attribution, trace sampling by latency), this is the API you write against, and the graph wiring is what guarantees your processor sees every signal exactly once.

Honest Limits

  • The core repo has no AI-specific components. Batching, tail sampling or prompt-scrubbing processors live in contrib (or in your own Go module). The core gives you the framework and a small stable set; the catalog is a separate dependency decision.
  • The service stanza is mandatory and strict. Validation requires at least one receiver and one exporter, and every reference must resolve — the empty-config errors are right there in config.go, L17.
  • The graph package is internal by design. You extend the Collector by implementing factories and components, not by editing the DAG; the flow shape is data-driven from config, which is a feature but also a constraint if you wanted exotic topologies.
  • The code moves fast. Every anchor in this post was verified against main on 2026-11-01; line numbers will drift, symbols less so. Treat the links as a snapshot.
  • No benchmarks here on purpose. The README’s own claims are qualitative — usable, performant, observable, extensible, unified — and I see no reason to invent numbers the project did not make.
  • Self-observability is real but easy to forget. The Host registers zPages endpoints (RegisterZPages, L110, rendering via HandleZPages, L21) that show the live graph and component status — turn them on before you need them at 3 a.m.

That is the whole journey: a cobra command, a config resolver, a graph builder, and a data model — four ideas that together route every trace, metric and log your AI stack will ever emit.
